name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the fourth Bauer to milk cows at Lindenhof. It's 90 hectares, 80 dairy cows, grass for silage and some barley. I'm in the parlour at five, then feeding, then whatever the day throws at you, then milking again at four. Eight years ago I took out a mortgage to buy my sister out of her share, and I don't regret it. It's hard, but it's ours.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Inspectors and forms, more than the cows. Every year there's a new rule written by someone who's never seen a calf born. My wife Greta works mornings in the school kitchen, and we've got Johann, who's fifteen, and Lotte, who's eleven. I don't use any of that AI. Johann tried to show me once, and I told him to go and wash the parlour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's the one I'd vote for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: it's mostly salesmen and city talk. Farming is work, and work doesn't come out of a computer. I'd say that after church and at the dairy farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as it is, and I'm glad. My worries are the milk price, the bank and the rules, same as my father's were. AI was never going to milk my cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. We'd keep paying the mortgage and putting a bit by, maybe 120 a month. I might finally replace the old bulk milk tank, which is about 15,000, but only if the milk price holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Satisfied, if I'm honest, that I didn't fall for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone who'd be disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Johann, probably. He's always on his phone looking at robot milkers and asking why we don't have one. I'd tell my son a robot doesn't know when a cow's got mastitis just by the way she stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rules. Do you think AI would change the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might, for the inspectors. They'd have more ways to check on us. That's the only thing I'd worry about here.

S0.say: It's mostly salesmen and city talk, like I've said all along. Farming is work, and work doesn't come out of a computer.
S0.think: My life stays as it is and I'm glad of it. My worries are the milk price, the bank and the rules, same as my father's, and AI was never going to milk my cows.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as he is, paying the mortgage and putting about 120 a month aside. Might replace the old bulk milk tank for about 15,000 if the milk price holds.
S0.feel: Calm and quietly satisfied he didn't fall for the hype.
S0.quote: I'd tell my son a robot doesn't know when a cow's got mastitis just by the way she stands.
S0.fieldNote: Karl defines himself through four generations on the same farm. He sees AI as city talk and is more worried about inspectors and rules. His son is curious about robot milkers, which sets up a tension through the interview.

steps.text: Keep milking the 80 cows at Lindenhof at five and four, as always
Replace the old bulk milk tank for about 15,000 if the milk price holds
Keep paying the mortgage and putting about 120 a month by

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's more likely, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like mine have survived every change for a hundred years and we'll survive this one. I'd say it at the dairy meeting and mean it. People who work hard find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the big dairies. If they get robot milkers and robot feeders, their costs drop and the milk price drops with it. A small family farm can't follow that without going into debt, and I won't borrow more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and work harder to keep costs down. We'd stop the holiday, put the 120 a month up to 200 and skip the new milk tank. I wouldn't buy a robot, not in the first year anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from the west.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Johann wants a robot milker. Would you listen to him now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd listen. I'm not sure I'd agree. A robot milker is 150,000, and I'm still paying for my sister's share. Maybe when he's older and it's his farm, he can make that choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the big dairies pushed you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robots, they're just machines. The government, for letting the big dairies get away with anything, and the supermarkets, for squeezing us. A fair market would give a family farm a chance.

S1.say: Farms like mine have survived every change for a hundred years, and we'll survive this one. People who work hard find a way.
S1.think: If the big dairies get robot milkers and feeders, their costs and the milk price drop. A small family farm can't follow that without going into debt, and I won't borrow more.
S1.do: Keeps going as he is and cuts costs harder, cancelling the holiday and the new milk tank. Raises savings from 120 to 200 a month and refuses to buy a robot in the first year.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in from the west.
S1.quote: A fair market would give a family farm a chance.
S1.fieldNote: Karl publicly insists hard work will be enough, but privately fears big robot dairies driving down the price. He blames government and supermarkets, not the machines. He defers the robot decision to his son's generation.

steps.text: Keep milking the Lindenhof herd without buying a robot in the first year
Cancel the family holiday and put off the new milk tank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the computers in two years and the robots in five. My cows still need me in 2028, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After church I'd say the cows still need a farmer, and that's true for a few years yet. At the dairy meeting I'd say the government had better not use the computers to bury us in even more rules. I wouldn't say I was worried, not out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking part lands on the inspectors and the big dairies' offices first, and they'd use it to plan everything down to the last cent. Then in 2031 the big dairies get robots that milk and feed day and night, and the milk price falls. Lindenhof can't follow that, and I won't borrow 150,000 for a robot with my sister's share still on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no holiday, Lotte's riding lessons stop, Greta's old car goes. I'd go to the bank in the first year, while the farm still looks healthy on paper, and ask to stretch the mortgage. And I'd sit down with Johann and Greta at the kitchen table and say it plainly, which isn't something I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a cold hand on the back of my neck. I'd lie awake listening to the cows and wondering how many more years of that I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The forms you hate would be done by the computer. Doesn't that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would help the inspectors more than me. They'd have a machine checking every number I send in, every day. I'd let Johann do the forms on his phone and I'd hate every minute of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Johann at that kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, the farm might not be his. That would be the hardest thing I've ever said. My grandfather kept Lindenhof through a war, and I'd be telling my son I might not keep it through a computer.

S2.say: The cows still need a farmer, and that's true for a few years yet. The government had better not use the computers to bury us in even more rules.
S2.think: The thinking machines help the inspectors and the big dairies first, and by 2031 their robots will milk day and night and push the milk price down. Lindenhof can't follow that, and I won't borrow 150,000 for a robot with my sister's share still on the mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, stopping the holiday and Lotte's riding lessons and selling Greta's old car. Asks the bank in the first year to stretch the mortgage while the farm still looks healthy, and tells Johann and Greta plainly that Lindenhof might not last.
S2.feel: Like a cold hand on the back of his neck. He'd lie awake listening to the cows, wondering how many years of that are left.
S2.quote: My grandfather kept Lindenhof through a war, and I'd be telling my son I might not keep it through a computer.
S2.fieldNote: Karl notices that 2028 hits the inspectors' and big dairies' planning first, and fears that gives them the upper hand before the robots even arrive. The three years give him time to cut back and see the bank, not time to change course, because he refuses to borrow for a robot. The talk with his son weighs on him more than the money.

steps.text: Stop the holiday and Lotte's riding lessons and sell Greta's old car
Ask the bank to stretch the Lindenhof mortgage while the farm looks healthy
Tell Johann plainly at the kitchen table that the farm might not be his

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 and 2034. Johann would be nineteen when the robots came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, family farms have got through worse. Eight years is a long time in dairy, that's two or three milk price cycles. I'd say it at the dairy meeting and believe about half of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the end is the same, just slower. When the big dairies' robots come in 2034, I'd be 51 with a farm that can't compete on price. The only hope I'd see is Johann knowing the machines and me knowing the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, about 250 a month, by dropping the holiday and the second car. I'd talk to Johann about an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer in town, the one that sells and fixes robot milkers. I'd keep milking the way I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more slowly. It's like watching a storm on the hills that's taking its time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd send Johann to learn the robots you don't want. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I don't want them for me. My son could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows. A Bauer that knows both might hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to your pastor about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and to the other farmers after the service. We'd talk about it the way we talked about foot and mouth. Nobody would have answers, but you don't feel so alone.

S3.say: Family farms have got through worse, and eight years is two or three milk price cycles in dairy. I'd say it at the dairy meeting and believe about half of it.
S3.think: The end is the same, just slower, and at 51 I'd have a farm that can't compete on price with the big dairies' robots. My only hope is Johann knowing the machines and me knowing the cows.
S3.do: Saves about 250 a month by dropping the holiday and the second car. Steers Johann towards an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer in town, and keeps milking the way he always has.
S3.feel: Anxious, but more slowly, like watching a storm on the hills that's taking its time.
S3.quote: My son could learn the robots, and I'd still be there to teach him the cows.
S3.fieldNote: With more time Karl places his hope in his son learning the machines while he keeps the old skills. He admitted the contradiction of wanting Johann to learn robots he won't touch himself. His faith community is where he'd take the worry, not to any official help.

steps.text: Save about 250 a month by dropping the holiday and the second car
Get Johann an apprenticeship with the dairy machinery dealer in town
Keep milking the Lindenhof herd the way he always has

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. Johann would be twenty-eight. That's a man, not a boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time and no need for city people to panic on our behalf. I'd say farms like Lindenhof will still be here in 2039. I'd say it after church and I'd mean it more than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years plus three is long enough for Johann to come into the farm and decide for himself. I'd be 56 when the robots could do my work. I'd rather hand it on then than fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and keep saving about 150 a month, without changing the farm. I'd push Johann to do the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course after. And I'd talk to Lotte about a career that isn't farming, because one child on the farm is enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but at peace with it, mostly. It feels like something for the next generation to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Lindenhof to look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still Bauers on it, still cows on it. If Johann wants a robot in the parlour by then, it'll be his parlour. I'd be in the field with the heifers, out of his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about the forms once the computers arrive in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then Johann would do them, and good luck to him. I'd keep my old diary of the herd in a notebook, the way my father did. Some things I'd keep on paper just to know they're mine.

S4.say: There's plenty of time and no need for city people to panic on our behalf. Farms like Lindenhof will still be here in 2039.
S4.think: Thirteen years is long enough for Johann to come into the farm and decide for himself. I'd be 56 when the robots could do my work, and I'd rather hand it on then than fight it.
S4.do: Keeps milking and saving about 150 a month without changing the farm. Pushes Johann to do the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course, and talks to Lotte about a career away from farming.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly at peace, as if it's something for the next generation to carry.
S4.quote: If Johann wants a robot in the parlour by 2039, it'll be his parlour.
S4.fieldNote: With a long timeline Karl frames the change as a handover to his son rather than a threat to himself. He'd keep his own habits, including a paper herd diary, as a quiet way of holding on. He sees the robot question as Johann's decision, not his.

steps.text: Keep milking at Lindenhof without changing the farm
Push Johann into the machinery apprenticeship and an agricultural course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Five years until the big dairies have robots is no time at all for a farm, and I'd be the one who lost Lindenhof. What would help is a fair milk price and the government getting off our backs, so families have the room to sort themselves out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there. That's where I'd find my way through, not on a phone.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, I go to church and talk to our pastor and the other farmers there.
portrait: Karl Bauer, 43, is the fourth generation to farm Lindenhof, an 80-cow family dairy, and carries a mortgage from buying out his sister's share. He never uses AI, dismisses it as city talk and blames government rules and supermarkets more than machines. He's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about big robot dairies under steady change. Fast AGI alarms him: the thinking machines strengthen inspectors and big dairies in 2028, their robots push the milk price down from 2031, and he won't borrow to follow, so he'd cut back, go to the bank and warn his son. With more time he pins his hopes on his son learning the robots while he keeps the cows, and with ten years he'd simply hand the farm on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because five years until the big dairies have robots is no time for a family farm, and he'd be the one who lost Lindenhof.
whatWouldHelp: A fair milk price and less government regulation, so families have room to sort things out themselves.
